{"answer": "# Funding and sustaining open scientific infrastructure

**Bottom line.** Open access is not cost-free operation. These services require continuing expenditure on expert curation, software maintenance, storage, security, user support, and governance. The literature finds a persistent mismatch: research grants are usually time-limited and reward new features, while trusted repositories and software need dependable funding for routine work over decades. The five named services illustrate different mixtures of public grants, institutional hosting, philanthropy, collective membership, and paid premium services; their published cost figures cover different years and activities and should not be compared as if they were equivalent annual budgets. (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000018, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000024)

## What the case studies actually cost and how they are funded

| Infrastructure | Documented cost or financial scale | Funding model and qualification |
|---|---|---|
| **arXiv** | Cornell projected **approximately US$550,000 for 2012** for six full-time-equivalent staff, servers, and networking; this is a historical *projection*, not a current audited budget. | Cornell University Library hosted it and planned to contribute **US$75,000 annually plus indirect expenses**. Its collective model sought support from roughly **200** heavily using libraries and research laboratories; four usage-based annual membership tiers were **US$1,500–3,000**, alongside Simons Foundation support. A later account described a goal of **at least US$300,000 per year** in membership income and five-year institutional commitments. These are historical model figures, not present-day operating costs. (pqac-00000044, pqac-00000045) |
| **Protein Data Bank (PDB)** | For **2023 US RCSB PDB operations**, federal grant amounts budgeted were approximately **US$2.8 million** for ingestion, validation, and biocuration; **US$2.2 million** for preservation; and **US$2.5 million** for dissemination—about **US$7.5 million across those three activities**. Corresponding estimates were **US$420 per newly processed structure**, **US$10.30 per archived structure per year**, and **US$0.30 per unique RCSB.org IP client**. These are *RCSB activity budgets*, not the worldwide PDB partnership’s consolidated accounts. | The US node is funded by **NSF, NIH, and DOE**; worldwide partner centers have separate European, Japanese, and other institutional and public funders. The archive remains free to use without usage restrictions. Its authors estimate aggregate preservation costs at about **1% of structure-determination costs**. PDB data also enabled AlphaFold2 and other protein-prediction work: AI depends on a previously funded, curated experimental corpus. (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000037, pqac-00000031) |
| **Zenodo** | A 2024 economic study models roughly **CHF 11 million in discounted development, maintenance, and operating costs over 2028–2057** for a comparable future platform. It estimates **CHF 2.8 billion in potential discounted socioeconomic benefit** over that period. **Neither is Zenodo’s observed annual budget or a realized return.** An independently verified current annual operating figure was not established in the material examined. | CERN hosts the free general-purpose repository, built on Invenio, with OpenAIRE and institutional support for its development and operation. Its integration with existing CERN technology and infrastructure is material to its cost structure. The economic study recommends that science-funding agencies and other beneficiaries invest in repositories and their quality, rather than expecting operators or depositors alone to bear the expense. (pqac-00000059, pqac-00000058, pqac-00000056) |
| **Open Science Framework (OSF)** | In a **2019 COS funding proposal**, the *Center for Open Science organization* reported an annual operating budget of **US$7 million**, with about **US$3 million** spent on product and engineering, approximately **35%** of the latter attributable to operations and maintenance. **US$7 million is not an OSF-only cost.** A separate COS proposal projected **US$229,225** to operate **26 OSF Preprints services in 2020**, for **33,650 papers**, or **US$6.81 per paper**; these too are proposal projections, not audited expenditure. | COS described a planned 2021 mix of **51% research grants, 39% philanthropy, and 10% earned revenue**, plus paid **OSF Institutions** memberships, federal contracts, and repository integrations to distribute storage costs. The cited NSF and CZI documents are *applications*: their requested budgets must not be described as awards. (pqac-00000048, pqac-00000047, pqac-00000049, pqac-00000052) |
| **OpenAlex** | The literature reports a **US$7.5 million Arcadia grant announced in 2024**, intended to help establish a sustainable open index over five years. **A grant total is not an annual operating-cost estimate**; the examined sources do not establish a comparable audited annual OpenAlex budget. | Nonprofit OurResearch combines grant and donation support with revenue from premium subscriptions and services. The bibliographic data remain openly reusable under **CC0**, while paying customers obtain higher-capacity access, more frequent updates, or support. An account of the 2026 API describes usage-based pricing and institutional tiers introduced for sustainability: an important distinction is between *open data* and unlimited, free, computationally expensive service. Long-run financial viability remains a question, not a demonstrated failure. (pqac-00000038, pqac-00000039, pqac-00000040) |

## What failure and retrenchment look like

The risk is documented, not merely theoretical. The ProteomeXchange consortium reported that **Tranche and Peptidome closed after NIH support ceased, with partial loss of data**. Another case study records **NIAID’s nonrenewal of VEuPathDB support in September 2024**; that support had covered approximately **60% of operating costs**. VEuPathDB continued with stopgap philanthropic and host support while developing tiered subscriptions. Thus, loss of a grant can mean a changed access model as well as a threatened shutdown. The same study documents a contrasting response: the Biodiversity Heritage Library formed a consortium and subsequently relied on organizational memberships, while MorphoBank adopted voluntary memberships but was still seeking enough support to meet its needs. (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016)

**Service reduction need not mean that the underlying platform disappears.** A 2024 examination of COS’s preprint ecosystem reported **29 listed preprint servers, 14 of which had ceased publishing or were no longer hosted by COS/OSF**, and discussed annual service charges as a possible contributor. That is a secondary account of *individual hosted services*, not evidence that the main OSF shut down or proof that every departure had the same cause. Repository dependencies can also fail more quietly when an API or data-release format changes, breaking downstream institutional workflows and creating new, often unbudgeted maintenance work. (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000018)

## Scientific software is part of the same infrastructure

Open-source scientific software often relies on grant-funded development and volunteer maintenance, even when many researchers or AI systems depend on it. A workshop report argues that paying indefinitely through sequential innovation grants is generally untenable; it proposes stable infrastructure-style funding, institutional membership, possible endowments, campus open-source coordination, research-software-engineer careers, and recognition of software in hiring and promotion. It also stresses an important limit: not *every* research script needs perpetual active maintenance; some should instead be documented and archived. A study of Astropy and research on grant-funded software transitions likewise treat community governance and maintainer succession—not merely preservation of code—as sustainability problems. (pqac-00000033, pqac-00000034, pqac-00000035, pqac-00000036)

Funder guidance recommends explicitly financing maintenance, documentation, governance, inclusive contributor communities, and scholarly credit, not only novel code. Fiscal sponsors and multi-project consortia can aggregate administrative work and fund paid maintainers; the Open Molecular Software Foundation’s collaboration across molecular-modeling projects is one proposed model. Such arrangements can combine public research grants, institutional resources, philanthropy, and industry contributions while keeping shared code open. (pqac-00000034, pqac-00000022)

## What changes as AI uses the commons

AI increases the *value* of curated open collections and can increase demand for machine-readable data, APIs, bulk transfer, and quality assurance. PDB’s role in protein-structure prediction is a concrete example of downstream AI value. Repository traffic also merits careful accounting: a PRIDE study of **159.3 million downloads in 2021–2025** classified **48.2% of traffic as automated bots** and found that bot traffic rose **sixteenfold**. **The study does not establish that those bots were generative-AI crawlers, or quantify the resulting bandwidth cost.** It does show why raw downloads are unreliable measures of human reuse and why capacity planning and bot-aware statistics matter. (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000060, pqac-00000062)

The strongest financing proposals follow from that distinction between an open *commons* and costly *services on top of it*:

1. **Fund recurring work explicitly.** Price curation, preservation, security, basic access, maintenance, and the organization that provides them separately from new-feature development. Hooft and Roos propose matching each activity to an appropriate payer: long-horizon public or host support for core operations; project grants for bounded development; partnerships for shared governance; and charges for genuinely high-marginal-cost premium services. They warn that deposit fees can disadvantage poorer institutions and cannot reliably finance perpetual care of previously deposited material. (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000024)
2. **Pool beneficiary contributions without making ordinary access contingent on payment.** arXiv’s library memberships, international biodata funder coordination, and domain-specific consortia illustrate collective support. Public agencies, universities, and large commercial or AI beneficiaries could contribute to common operating funds; differentiated high-volume API or service charges are a *policy option*, not a proven universal solution or a claim that free reuse should end. The literature also notes that full government funding or an endowment could provide continuity, but both are difficult to secure in practice. (pqac-00000044, pqac-00000012, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000024, pqac-00000034)
3. **Reduce avoidable machine-use costs and protect openness.** Provide documented bulk snapshots, caching or mirrors, sensible API tiers, and bot-aware metrics so automated users need not repeatedly scrape interactive services. Retain openly reusable datasets, interoperable identifiers, preservation and exit plans, and community oversight; charging for high-capacity computation is different from enclosing the underlying scholarly record. These are recommendations inferred from documented usage patterns and the OpenAlex model, **not measured savings for all five platforms**. (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000040, pqac-00000060, pqac-00000065, pqac-00000003)

**Assessment.** The most defensible conclusion is not that one revenue model will sustain every service. {"answer": "# Funding and sustaining open scientific infrastructure

**Bottom line.** Open access is not cost-free operation. These services require continuing expenditure on expert curation, software maintenance, storage, security, user support, and governance. The literature finds a persistent mismatch: research grants are usually time-limited and reward new features, while trusted repositories and software need dependable funding for routine work over decades. The five named services illustrate different mixtures of public grants, institutional hosting, philanthropy, collective membership, and paid premium services; their published cost figures cover different years and activities and should not be compared as if they were equivalent annual budgets. (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000018, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000024)

## What the case studies actually cost and how they are funded

| Infrastructure | Documented cost or financial scale | Funding model and qualification |
|---|---|---|
| **arXiv** | Cornell projected **approximately US$550,000 for 2012** for six full-time-equivalent staff, servers, and networking; this is a historical *projection*, not a current audited budget. | Cornell University Library hosted it and planned to contribute **US$75,000 annually plus indirect expenses**. Its collective model sought support from roughly **200** heavily using libraries and research laboratories; four usage-based annual membership tiers were **US$1,500–3,000**, alongside Simons Foundation support. A later account described a goal of **at least US$300,000 per year** in membership income and five-year institutional commitments. These are historical model figures, not present-day operating costs. (pqac-00000044, pqac-00000045) |
| **Protein Data Bank (PDB)** | For **2023 US RCSB PDB operations**, federal grant amounts budgeted were approximately **US$2.8 million** for ingestion, validation, and biocuration; **US$2.2 million** for preservation; and **US$2.5 million** for dissemination—about **US$7.5 million across those three activities**. Corresponding estimates were **US$420 per newly processed structure**, **US$10.30 per archived structure per year**, and **US$0.30 per unique RCSB.org IP client**. These are *RCSB activity budgets*, not the worldwide PDB partnership’s consolidated accounts. | The US node is funded by **NSF, NIH, and DOE**; worldwide partner centers have separate European, Japanese, and other institutional and public funders. The archive remains free to use without usage restrictions. Its authors estimate aggregate preservation costs at about **1% of structure-determination costs**. PDB data also enabled AlphaFold2 and other protein-prediction work: AI depends on a previously funded, curated experimental corpus. (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000037, pqac-00000031) |
| **Zenodo** | A 2024 economic study models roughly **CHF 11 million in discounted development, maintenance, and operating costs over 2028–2057** for a comparable future platform. It estimates **CHF 2.8 billion in potential discounted socioeconomic benefit** over that period. **Neither is Zenodo’s observed annual budget or a realized return.** An independently verified current annual operating figure was not established in the material examined. | CERN hosts the free general-purpose repository, built on Invenio, with OpenAIRE and institutional support for its development and operation. Its integration with existing CERN technology and infrastructure is material to its cost structure. The economic study recommends that science-funding agencies and other beneficiaries invest in repositories and their quality, rather than expecting operators or depositors alone to bear the expense. (pqac-00000059, pqac-00000058, pqac-00000056) |
| **Open Science Framework (OSF)** | In a **2019 COS funding proposal**, the *Center for Open Science organization* reported an annual operating budget of **US$7 million**, with about **US$3 million** spent on product and engineering, approximately **35%** of the latter attributable to operations and maintenance. **US$7 million is not an OSF-only cost.** A separate COS proposal projected **US$229,225** to operate **26 OSF Preprints services in 2020**, for **33,650 papers**, or **US$6.81 per paper**; these too are proposal projections, not audited expenditure. | COS described a planned 2021 mix of **51% research grants, 39% philanthropy, and 10% earned revenue**, plus paid **OSF Institutions** memberships, federal contracts, and repository integrations to distribute storage costs. The cited NSF and CZI documents are *applications*: their requested budgets must not be described as awards. (pqac-00000048, pqac-00000047, pqac-00000049, pqac-00000052) |
| **OpenAlex** | The literature reports a **US$7.5 million Arcadia grant announced in 2024**, intended to help establish a sustainable open index over five years. **A grant total is not an annual operating-cost estimate**; the examined sources do not establish a comparable audited annual OpenAlex budget. | Nonprofit OurResearch combines grant and donation support with revenue from premium subscriptions and services. The bibliographic data remain openly reusable under **CC0**, while paying customers obtain higher-capacity access, more frequent updates, or support. An account of the 2026 API describes usage-based pricing and institutional tiers introduced for sustainability: an important distinction is between *open data* and unlimited, free, computationally expensive service. Long-run financial viability remains a question, not a demonstrated failure. (pqac-00000038, pqac-00000039, pqac-00000040) |

## What failure and retrenchment look like

The risk is documented, not merely theoretical. The ProteomeXchange consortium reported that **Tranche and Peptidome closed after NIH support ceased, with partial loss of data**. Another case study records **NIAID’s nonrenewal of VEuPathDB support in September 2024**; that support had covered approximately **60% of operating costs**. VEuPathDB continued with stopgap philanthropic and host support while developing tiered subscriptions. Thus, loss of a grant can mean a changed access model as well as a threatened shutdown. The same study documents a contrasting response: the Biodiversity Heritage Library formed a consortium and subsequently relied on organizational memberships, while MorphoBank adopted voluntary memberships but was still seeking enough support to meet its needs. (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016)

**Service reduction need not mean that the underlying platform disappears.** A 2024 examination of COS’s preprint ecosystem reported **29 listed preprint servers, 14 of which had ceased publishing or were no longer hosted by COS/OSF**, and discussed annual service charges as a possible contributor. That is a secondary account of *individual hosted services*, not evidence that the main OSF shut down or proof that every departure had the same cause. Repository dependencies can also fail more quietly when an API or data-release format changes, breaking downstream institutional workflows and creating new, often unbudgeted maintenance work. (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000018)

## Scientific software is part of the same infrastructure

Open-source scientific software often relies on grant-funded development and volunteer maintenance, even when many researchers or AI systems depend on it. A workshop report argues that paying indefinitely through sequential innovation grants is generally untenable; it proposes stable infrastructure-style funding, institutional membership, possible endowments, campus open-source coordination, research-software-engineer careers, and recognition of software in hiring and promotion. It also stresses an important limit: not *every* research script needs perpetual active maintenance; some should instead be documented and archived. A study of Astropy and research on grant-funded software transitions likewise treat community governance and maintainer succession—not merely preservation of code—as sustainability problems. (pqac-00000033, pqac-00000034, pqac-00000035, pqac-00000036)

Funder guidance recommends explicitly financing maintenance, documentation, governance, inclusive contributor communities, and scholarly credit, not only novel code. Fiscal sponsors and multi-project consortia can aggregate administrative work and fund paid maintainers; the Open Molecular Software Foundation’s collaboration across molecular-modeling projects is one proposed model. Such arrangements can combine public research grants, institutional resources, philanthropy, and industry contributions while keeping shared code open. (pqac-00000034, pqac-00000022)

## What changes as AI uses the commons

AI increases the *value* of curated open collections and can increase demand for machine-readable data, APIs, bulk transfer, and quality assurance. PDB’s role in protein-structure prediction is a concrete example of downstream AI value. Repository traffic also merits careful accounting: a PRIDE study of **159.3 million downloads in 2021–2025** classified **48.2% of traffic as automated bots** and found that bot traffic rose **sixteenfold**. **The study does not establish that those bots were generative-AI crawlers, or quantify the resulting bandwidth cost.** It does show why raw downloads are unreliable measures of human reuse and why capacity planning and bot-aware statistics matter. (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000060, pqac-00000062)

The strongest financing proposals follow from that distinction between an open *commons* and costly *services on top of it*:

1. **Fund recurring work explicitly.** Price curation, preservation, security, basic access, maintenance, and the organization that provides them separately from new-feature development. Hooft and Roos propose matching each activity to an appropriate payer: long-horizon public or host support for core operations; project grants for bounded development; partnerships for shared governance; and charges for genuinely high-marginal-cost premium services. They warn that deposit fees can disadvantage poorer institutions and cannot reliably finance perpetual care of previously deposited material. (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000024)
2. **Pool beneficiary contributions without making ordinary access contingent on payment.** arXiv’s library memberships, international biodata funder coordination, and domain-specific consortia illustrate collective support. Public agencies, universities, and large commercial or AI beneficiaries could contribute to common operating funds; differentiated high-volume API or service charges are a *policy option*, not a proven universal solution or a claim that free reuse should end. The literature also notes that full government funding or an endowment could provide continuity, but both are difficult to secure in practice. (pqac-00000044, pqac-00000012, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000024, pqac-00000034)
3. **Reduce avoidable machine-use costs and protect openness.** Provide documented bulk snapshots, caching or mirrors, sensible API tiers, and bot-aware metrics so automated users need not repeatedly scrape interactive services. Retain openly reusable datasets, interoperable identifiers, preservation and exit plans, and community oversight; charging for high-capacity computation is different from enclosing the underlying scholarly record. These are recommendations inferred from documented usage patterns and the OpenAlex model, **not measured savings for all five platforms**. (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000040, pqac-00000060, pqac-00000065, pqac-00000003)

**Assessment.** The most defensible conclusion is not that one revenue model will sustain every service. It is that grant-funded expansion, library or institutional stewardship, international consortia, philanthropy, potential endowment income, and paid high-cost services each finance different parts of the lifecycle. Long-term obligations need long-term commitments, transparent activity-level accounts, and governance that keeps the scientific commons accessible even when AI and other intensive users increase demand. (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000021, pqac-00000024, pqac-00000034)"}

## What changes as AI uses the commons

AI increases the *value* of curated open collections and can increase demand for machine-readable data, APIs, bulk transfer, and quality assurance. contexts.context: Hooft and Roos (2025) argue that research data services often emerge from time-limited projects and risk discontinuation afterward. Sustainability requires both technical maintainability and financial planning, yet “very little” dedicated infrastructure funding exists. Sustainability depends on purpose, users, impact, adaptability, and institutional adoption. contexts.context: The literature warns that free services create a “tragedy of the commons”: non-members benefit, so memberships need incentives such as governance influence or international collaboration. User subscriptions could force researchers to maintain “dozens” of services, creating overhead and monopoly risks. Short-term grants rarely fund dependable operations: projects reach TRL 3–4, while usable services require TRL 6–7, leaving good implementations abandoned or redundantly rebuilt. Sustainability should therefore combine funding sources by activity—service development, infrastructure operations, and organisational maintenance—using early activity-based cost analysis; no single model covers all needs.

Short-term grants cannot sustain long-term operations through “overheads.” One-off “seed” funding is often mislabeled public infrastructure funding; ELIXIR reports “very few” dedicated long-term schemes. Underfunding risks decay, service unreliability, repeated reinvention, and lost user trust.

The excerpt does not provide the exact $7.5 million Arcadia grant, premium-services subscription cost, detailed API funding arrangements, hybrid funding information from “OpenAlex Big Three,” or Zenodo’s financial sponsorship scale and limits. contexts.context: The excerpt does not contain the Zenodo 2024 paper “Value of an Open Scientific Data and Documentation Platform,” nor does it report that platform’s actual annual operating costs, CERN/OpenAIRE funding, or forecast socioeconomic benefit. It does, however, provide a useful conceptual distinction for interpreting such figures: operating or access costs are not the same as the economic value generated by an open-data platform. The review describes access costs as time-related expenditures incurred by users, while broader impact estimates may use willingness to pay, willingness to accept, direct use value, or estimated efficiency savings. These measures can differ substantially. For example, the British Atmospheric Data Centre is associated with estimated annual access costs of £2.3 million, willingness to pay of about £5.2 million, willingness to accept of about £15 million, and potential efficiency impacts ranging from £10 million to £58 million. The text emphasizes that these are distinct perspectives on value and that comparability and validity can be challenging. Therefore, the requested Zenodo paper’s budget/funding figures should be treated as actual resource requirements, while its forecast socioeconomic benefit should be treated as an impact-model output rather than as the platform’s operating budget.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides evidence that automated traffic is a material confounder for scholarly-repository usage metrics, although it does not specifically identify AI-related bots or demonstrate an increase over time. It cites an external estimate that bots constitute 30%–70% of all internet traffic and argues that open scientific repositories such as PRIDE are attractive targets because of their accessible, valuable content. The documented empirical consequence is metric distortion: unfiltered bot activity can inflate apparent download counts and therefore bias assessments of repository impact and dataset reuse. The excerpt also describes PRIDE’s empirical response: processing five years of anonymized logs (January 2021–December 2025), yielding 159,327,635 download records, with a workflow that removes incomplete transfers and inconsistencies and a machine-learning system, DeepLogBot, that classifies traffic into bots, institutional download hubs, and other categories. These methods support more reliable usage measurement, but the passage reports no direct evidence that AI-driven scraping increased PRIDE traffic, consumed additional capacity, or threatened sustainability. Statements about download analytics becoming increasingly important are forward-looking projections or motivations, not measured effects. Likewise, the 30%–70% figure is a broad internet-wide estimate, not a PRIDE-specific measurement.

answer.formatted_answer:
Question: What does the literature say about the funding and sustainability of open scholarly and scientific infrastructure (arXiv, the Protein Data Bank, Zenodo, OSF, OpenAlex, community open-source scientific software)? Include costs, funding models (grants, memberships, consortia, endowments), documented failures or service reductions, and proposals for sustaining such infrastructure as AI increases its use.

# Funding and sustaining open scientific infrastructure

**Bottom line.** Open access is not cost-free operation. These services require continuing expenditure on expert curation, software maintenance, storage, security, user support, and governance. The literature finds a persistent mismatch: research grants are usually time-limited and reward new features, while trusted repositories and software need dependable funding for routine work over decades. The five named services illustrate different mixtures of public grants, institutional hosting, philanthropy, collective membership, and paid premium services; their published cost figures cover different years and activities and should not be compared as if they were equivalent annual budgets. (hooft2025financingmodelsfor pages 1-3, hooft2025financingmodelsfor pages 3-4, hooft2025financingmodelsfor pages 6-8, hooft2025financingmodelsfor pages 14-16)

## What the case studies actually cost and how they are funded

| Infrastructure | Documented cost or financial scale | Funding model and qualification |
|---|---|---|
| **arXiv** | Cornell projected **approximately US$550,000 for 2012** for six full-time-equivalent staff, servers, and networking; this is a historical *projection*, not a current audited budget. | Cornell University Library hosted it and planned to contribute **US$75,000 annually plus indirect expenses**. Its collective model sought support from roughly **200** heavily using libraries and research laboratories; four usage-based annual membership tiers were **US$1,500–3,000**, alongside Simons Foundation support. A later account described a goal of **at least US$300,000 per year** in membership income and five-year institutional commitments. These are historical model figures, not present-day operating costs. (rieger2015sustainabilityscholarlyrepository pages 1-3, reinsfelder2018usinglibraryfunds pages 9-14) |
| **Protein Data Bank (PDB)** | For **2023 US RCSB PDB operations**, federal grant amounts budgeted were approximately **US$2.8 million** for ingestion, validation, and biocuration; **US$2.2 million** for preservation; and **US$2.5 million** for dissemination—about **US$7.5 million across those three activities**. Corresponding estimates were **US$420 per newly processed structure**, **US$10.30 per archived structure per year**, and **US$0.30 per unique RCSB.org IP client**. These are *RCSB activity budgets*, not the worldwide PDB partnership’s consolidated accounts. | The US node is funded by **NSF, NIH, and DOE**; worldwide partner centers have separate European, Japanese, and other institutional and public funders. The archive remains free to use without usage restrictions. Its authors estimate aggregate preservation costs at about **1% of structure-determination costs**. PDB data also enabled AlphaFold2 and other protein-prediction work: AI depends on a previously funded, curated experimental corpus. (berman2025proteindatabank pages 6-7, berman2025proteindatabank media ca37aa27, berman2025proteindatabank pages 8-10) |
| **Zenodo** | A 2024 economic study models roughly **CHF 11 million in discounted development, maintenance, and operating costs over 2028–2057** for a comparable future platform. It estimates **CHF 2.8 billion in potential discounted socioeconomic benefit** over that period. **Neither is Zenodo’s observed annual budget or a realized return.** An independently verified current annual operating figure was not established in the material examined. | CERN hosts the free general-purpose repository, built on Invenio, with OpenAIRE and institutional support for its development and operation. Its integration with existing CERN technology and infrastructure is material to its cost structure. The economic study recommends that science-funding agencies and other beneficiaries invest in repositories and their quality, rather than expecting operators or depositors alone to bear the expense. (garrido2024thevalueof pages 1-3, garrido2024thevalueof pages 6-9, garrido2024thevalueof pages 18-20) |
| **Open Science Framework (OSF)** | In a **2019 COS funding proposal**, the *Center for Open Science organization* reported an annual operating budget of **US$7 million**, with about **US$3 million** spent on product and engineering, approximately **35%** of the latter attributable to operations and maintenance. **US$7 million is not an OSF-only cost.** A separate COS proposal projected **US$229,225** to operate **26 OSF Preprints services in 2020**, for **33,650 papers**, or **US$6.81 per paper**; these too are proposal projections, not audited expenditure. | COS described a planned 2021 mix of **51% research grants, 39% philanthropy, and 10% earned revenue**, plus paid **OSF Institutions** memberships, federal contracts, and repository integrations to distribute storage costs. The cited NSF and CZI documents are *applications*: their requested budgets must not be described as awards. (nosek2019centerforopen pages 19-21, schroederUnknownyear…initiative(czi) pages 1-4, nosek2019centerforopen pages 1-3, nosek2019centerforopen pages 13-15) |
| **OpenAlex** | The literature reports a **US$7.5 million Arcadia grant announced in 2024**, intended to help establish a sustainable open index over five years. **A grant total is not an annual operating-cost estimate**; the examined sources do not establish a comparable audited annual OpenAlex budget. | Nonprofit OurResearch combines grant and donation support with revenue from premium subscriptions and services. The bibliographic data remain openly reusable under **CC0**, while paying customers obtain higher-capacity access, more frequent updates, or support. An account of the 2026 API describes usage-based pricing and institutional tiers introduced for sustainability: an important distinction is between *open data* and unlimited, free, computationally expensive service. Long-run financial viability remains a question, not a demonstrated failure. (torressalinas2601thebigthree pages 8-10, borrego2512openalexfeaturesadvantages pages 1-2, domenighetti2026optimizingthemonitoringc pages 59-62) |

## What failure and retrenchment look like

The risk is documented, not merely theoretical. The ProteomeXchange consortium reported that **Tranche and Peptidome closed after NIH support ceased, with partial loss of data**. Another case study records **NIAID’s nonrenewal of VEuPathDB support in September 2024**; that support had covered approximately **60% of operating costs**. VEuPathDB continued with stopgap philanthropic and host support while developing tiered subscriptions. Thus, loss of a grant can mean a changed access model as well as a threatened shutdown. The same study documents a contrasting response: the Biodiversity Heritage Library formed a consortium and subsequently relied on organizational memberships, while MorphoBank adopted voluntary memberships but was still seeking enough support to meet its needs. (imker2025sustainabilityduringinstability pages 1-4, imker2025sustainabilityduringinstability pages 8-11, imker2025sustainabilityduringinstability pages 11-13)

**Service reduction need not mean that the underlying platform disappears.** A 2024 examination of COS’s preprint ecosystem reported **29 listed preprint servers, 14 of which had ceased publishing or were no longer hosted by COS/OSF**, and discussed annual service charges as a possible contributor. That is a secondary account of *individual hosted services*, not evidence that the main OSF shut down or proof that every departure had the same cause. Repository dependencies can also fail more quietly when an API or data-release format changes, breaking downstream institutional workflows and creating new, often unbudgeted maintenance work. (domenighetti2026optimizingthemonitoring pages 78-81, hooft2025financingmodelsfor pages 3-4)

## Scientific software is part of the same infrastructure

Open-source scientific software often relies on grant-funded development and volunteer maintenance, even when many researchers or AI systems depend on it. A workshop report argues that paying indefinitely through sequential innovation grants is generally untenable; it proposes stable infrastructure-style funding, institutional membership, possible endowments, campus open-source coordination, research-software-engineer careers, and recognition of software in hiring and promotion. It also stresses an important limit: not *every* research script needs perpetual active maintenance; some should instead be documented and archived. A study of Astropy and research on grant-funded software transitions likewise treat community governance and maintainer succession—not merely preservation of code—as sustainability problems. (mccracken2026sustainingopensource pages 6-9, mccracken2026sustainingopensource pages 9-12, mccracken2026sustainingopensource pages 12-16, mccracken2026sustainingopensource pages 16-19)

Funder guidance recommends explicitly financing maintenance, documentation, governance, inclusive contributor communities, and scholarly credit, not only novel code. Fiscal sponsors and multi-project consortia can aggregate administrative work and fund paid maintainers; the Open Molecular Software Foundation’s collaboration across molecular-modeling projects is one proposed model. Such arrangements can combine public research grants, institutional resources, philanthropy, and industry contributions while keeping shared code open. (mccracken2026sustainingopensource pages 9-12, hooft2025financingmodelsfor pages 10-12)

## What changes as AI uses the commons

AI increases the *value* of curated open collections and can increase demand for machine-readable data, APIs, bulk transfer, and quality assurance. PDB’s role in protein-structure prediction is a concrete example of downstream AI value. Repository traffic also merits careful accounting: a PRIDE study of **159.3 million downloads in 2021–2025** classified **48.2% of traffic as automated bots** and found that bot traffic rose **sixteenfold**. **The study does not establish that those bots were generative-AI crawlers, or quantify the resulting bandwidth cost.** It does show why raw downloads are unreliable measures of human reuse and why capacity planning and bot-aware statistics matter. (berman2025proteindatabank pages 8-10, hewapathirana2026quantifyingdatareuse pages 7-7, hewapathirana2026quantifyingdatareuse pages 4-4)

The strongest financing proposals follow from that distinction between an open *commons* and costly *services on top of it*:

1. **Fund recurring work explicitly.** Price curation, preservation, security, basic access, maintenance, and the organization that provides them separately from new-feature development. Hooft and Roos propose matching each activity to an appropriate payer: long-horizon public or host support for core operations; project grants for bounded development; partnerships for shared governance; and charges for genuinely high-marginal-cost premium services. They warn that deposit fees can disadvantage poorer institutions and cannot reliably finance perpetual care of previously deposited material. (hooft2025financingmodelsfor pages 4-6, hooft2025financingmodelsfor pages 6-8, hooft2025financingmodelsfor pages 8-10, hooft2025financingmodelsfor pages 10-12, hooft2025financingmodelsfor pages 12-14, hooft2025financingmodelsfor pages 14-16)
2. **Pool beneficiary contributions without making ordinary access contingent on payment.** arXiv’s library memberships, international biodata funder coordination, and domain-specific consortia illustrate collective support. Public agencies, universities, and large commercial or AI beneficiaries could contribute to common operating funds; differentiated high-volume API or service charges are a *policy option*, not a proven universal solution or a claim that free reuse should end. The literature also notes that full government funding or an endowment could provide continuity, but both are difficult to secure in practice. (rieger2015sustainabilityscholarlyrepository pages 1-3, imker2025sustainabilityduringinstability pages 1-4, hooft2025financingmodelsfor pages 10-12, hooft2025financingmodelsfor pages 14-16, mccracken2026sustainingopensource pages 9-12)
3. **Reduce avoidable machine-use costs and protect openness.** Provide documented bulk snapshots, caching or mirrors, sensible API tiers, and bot-aware metrics so automated users need not repeatedly scrape interactive services. Retain openly reusable datasets, interoperable identifiers, preservation and exit plans, and community oversight; charging for high-capacity computation is different from enclosing the underlying scholarly record. These are recommendations inferred from documented usage patterns and the OpenAlex model, **not measured savings for all five platforms**. (borrego2512openalexfeaturesadvantages pages 1-2, domenighetti2026optimizingthemonitoringc pages 59-62, hewapathirana2026quantifyingdatareuse pages 7-7, hewapathirana2026quantifyingdatareuse pages 7-8, mabile2025recommendationsonopen pages 6-7)

**Assessment.** The most defensible conclusion is not that one revenue model will sustain every service. It is that grant-funded expansion, library or institutional stewardship, international consortia, philanthropy, potential endowment income, and paid high-cost services each finance different parts of the lifecycle. Long-term obligations need long-term commitments, transparent activity-level accounts, and governance that keeps the scientific commons accessible even when AI and other intensive users increase demand. (hooft2025financingmodelsfor pages 3-4, hooft2025financingmodelsfor pages 8-10, hooft2025financingmodelsfor pages 14-16, mccracken2026sustainingopensource pages 9-12)
